Epilepsy is a long-term neurological disorder that affects
about 1% of people worldwide. It causes repeated seizures due
to abnormal brain activity. Fast and accurate seizure detection
is essential for diagnosis, treatment adjustments, and patient
safety [1]. EEG is a non-invasive and affordable tool for
recording brain activity. However, doctors often find it tiring
and subjective to visually inspect EEG signals, especially
with long-term monitoring data. Early methods of automated
seizure detection relied on handcrafted features from wavelet
transforms, Fourier analysis, or statistical measures. These
features were used in traditional classifiers like SVM, Decision
Trees, or Random Forests. While these models performed well
on specific datasets, they had difficulty managing the high
variability in EEG data between different individuals.
Recently, deep learning has emerged as a powerful option.
Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Recurrent Neural
Networks (RNNs) can automatically spot patterns without
needing explicit feature engineering [2]. However, many current models require a lot of computing power and are not
suitable for real-time or embedded systems.

Earlier studies in seizure detection relied on handcrafted
features and traditional classifiers. For example, Subasi (2007)
used wavelet decomposition followed by neural networks [3].
Tzallas et al. (2009) extracted time-frequency features and
combined them with SVMs for identifying seizures [4]. While
these methods achieved reasonable accuracy within subjects,
they depended heavily on expert feature design and did not
perform well across different subjects.
With the rise of deep learning, models started to learn
complex EEG patterns directly from raw or preprocessed
data. Ullah et al. (2018) created a CNN-LSTM hybrid that
achieved impressive accuracy on the Bonn and CHB-MIT
datasets [2]. Acharya et al. (2019) introduced a 13-layer CNN
that automated feature extraction from raw EEG. Lawhern
et al. (2018) presented EEGNet, which used depthwise and
separable convolutions to form an efficient design suitable for
various EEG tasks [5]. Despite their success, most existing
models have concentrated on validating their results within the
same subject, which limits their reliability in clinical settings.

This work uses EEG recordings from the Siena Scalp EEG
Dataset [6], which tracks brain activity in 14 people with
epilepsy. Each patient wore 29 scalp electrodes, recording at
512 Hz, for about 128 hours in total.
